name: Diffuser curl drying

lead: Diffuser curl drying means drying hair with a wide attachment that spreads the dryer's airflow, so curly, wavy, permed or fine hair keeps defined curls with added volume. Users say it cuts frizz compared with blasting hair with a bare dryer.

Dryer references describe a diffuser as spreading the air so hair dries more slowly, at a lower temperature and with less disturbance, which is said to reduce frizz and add volume. The result is visible once hair is dry and lasts until the next wash. No clinical studies of diffusing were found.

paras: People apply their usual curl products to damp hair, then hold sections of hair in the diffuser bowl or move it around the head on low or medium speed and heat. It is used on wash days in place of air-drying or a bare nozzle. Drying time is longer than with a standard nozzle.
Heat from dryers can leave hair dry and brittle with heavy use, according to hair-care references. No other specific hazards were reported.

web.title: How to Diffuse Your Hair, According to Hairstylists

angle.text: A diffuser dries curly, wavy or fine hair with softer, spread-out airflow, so curls look more defined, less frizzy and fuller. The look is visible once hair is dry and lasts until the next wash.

lead: Diffuser curl drying is the practice of drying hair with a hair-dryer attachment that spreads the airflow, so that curls and waves keep their shape and dry with more definition and volume instead of being blown into frizz. People with naturally curly, wavy, permed or fine hair use it to get a styled, defined head of hair without air-drying for hours. [1][2]

Dryer references describe the diffuser as spreading the air so hair is not blown around while it dries; drying is slower and cooler, which is said to reduce frizz and add volume. [1] Stylists quoted in the press say it helps define curls and covers a larger area than a standard blow-dry, and that technique varies with curl pattern. [2]

For looks, the payoff is hair texture: a clearly formed curl pattern, root lift and less fuzz make hair look fuller and more deliberately styled, which many people treat as part of overall grooming. The effect lasts until the next wash. No clinical trial has tested diffusing for curl definition.
infobox: Curly, wavy, permed, fine or colored hair [1]
Less frizz, added volume, curl definition [1][2]

paras: A hair dryer blows air from a fan over a heating element. Alongside the diffuser, common attachments include a concentrator nozzle that narrows airflow to dry faster and a comb nozzle, which is a concentrator with teeth. [1] Diffusers spread the air over a wider area instead of directing it as a single stream. [1]

Dryers themselves date to 1888, when French stylist Alexandre Godefroy built a seated bonnet dryer for his Paris salon, and handheld household models appeared around 1920. [1] Many modern dryers advertise ceramic elements or ionic operation; the effectiveness of ionic dryers is described as debated. [1]

Styling with dryers is described as forming temporary hydrogen bonds in the hair, which humidity and washing undo. [1] Proponents of diffusing say the gentler airflow dries curls without scattering them, which they associate with less frizz and more volume.

In a Yahoo News piece, celebrity hairstylist Clariss Rubenstein said coily hair benefits from twisting before diffusing so curls do not separate, and suggested combing, scrunching and then diffusing for wavy hair. Trichologist Shab Reslan said the process works on damp hair after product is applied. [2] Both described working in sections rather than moving the diffuser constantly, since constant movement is said to cause frizz and less consistent curls. [2]

Hair-brand and salon sites describe variations such as hover diffusing, which avoids touching the hair, and upside-down diffusing, used for root lift. These are stylist and brand descriptions rather than studied techniques.

General hair-care references note that hair ends overheated by dryers and hot irons can become dry and brittle, and that permed hair should be treated more gently than untreated hair. [3] Reslan advised keeping both speed and heat as low as possible, even though drying takes longer, and said high heat or powerful airflow can disrupt the hair cuticle. [2] Stylists commonly recommend medium or low heat and a heat protectant.
